title: Saturn's New Decagon: A Giant 10-Sided Mystery
summary:
Imagine a storm so big it wraps around an entire planet, and it's shaped like a perfect decagon—a 10-sided polygon. That's exactly what NASA's Hubble Space Telescope has spotted swirling around Saturn's south pole. It's the first time scientists have seen such a large, regularly shaped jet pattern in Saturn's southern hemisphere, and it's a total mystery.

Saturn already boasts a famous hexagon (a six-sided shape) at its north pole, a feature that has persisted for over 40 years. But this new decagon is different. It appears to be strengthening, giving scientists a rare chance to watch a giant atmospheric pattern develop in real time. "The northern hexagon has been there every time we've looked for more than 40 years. This feature is different—it appears to be strengthening," said one researcher.

The discovery began with amateur astronomers. In 2024, they noticed a faint, wavy band near Saturn's south pole in ground-based images. By 2025, the feature had developed into a clear decagon. Lead author Agustín Sánchez-Lavega, from the University of the Basque Country in Spain, then turned to Hubble for a sharper view. Hubble orbits above Earth's atmosphere, so it can capture crisp images without the blurring that ground telescopes suffer.

Sánchez-Lavega and his team have been searching for a southern counterpart to the hexagon since 1990, but even NASA's Cassini spacecraft, which orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, showed no sign of one. Now, suddenly, this decagon has appeared. It lies within one of Saturn's powerful jet streams and extends through several atmospheric layers, meaning it's not just a surface pattern.

The most intriguing part? No one knows why it formed now. "The question is, why did it suddenly form now when we haven't seen one before?" said Simon. Scientists will use Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope, along with computer models, to figure out how it formed and whether it will last.

This discovery highlights the value of Hubble's long operational history. The OPAL program has been capturing annual images of outer planets for over a decade, allowing scientists to monitor seasonal changes and spot patterns that develop gradually. Saturn's changing seasons played a role, as its south pole became visible from Earth again. What will Saturn reveal next? Only time—and more observations—will tell.
why_it_matters: Understanding Saturn's mysterious jet patterns helps scientists learn how atmospheres move on giant planets, and those same physical rules shape weather and climate models used for planets including Earth. It also shows what can be discovered by keeping scientific instruments like Hubble working for decades.

background_read: Saturn is a giant planet made mostly of gas, and its atmosphere has fast, narrow wind bands known as jet streams.
Saturn's north pole has hosted a six-sided hexagon for many years, a pattern first noticed decades ago by NASA's Voyager spacecraft and still present whenever telescopes look.
This new story focuses on the south pole, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope — an orbiting observatory that takes sharper images than ground telescopes because it sits above the blurring atmosphere.
The research team is led by Agustín Sánchez-Lavega, a planetary scientist at the University of the Basque Country in Spain.

Hubble's OPAL program (Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy) has photographed the outer planets nearly every year for over a decade, and because Saturn's south pole has become visible again from Earth, that long record can catch slowly changing seasonal features such as the emerging decagon.

perspectives.description: Scientists are excited because they are watching a new giant atmospheric pattern form in real time, which is extremely rare. The strengthening decagon gives them a natural laboratory for testing ideas about jet streams and planetary weather.

No one can yet explain why the decagon formed now, so confident claims about Saturn's atmosphere are limited. If the pattern fades quickly, it may turn out to be a temporary seasonal ripple rather than a lasting feature, showing how much remains unknown.

Giant planets have layered atmospheres shaped by rotation, sunlight, and internal heat, and Saturn's long seasons likely play a role. The decagon may reflect seasonal heating now that the south pole is getting more sunlight, but only repeated observations can confirm that pattern.

With Hubble, the James Webb Space Telescope, and computer models, scientists can now watch whether the decagon strengthens, fades, or moves. Future observations will test whether similar multi-sided patterns appear on other planets or at other points in Saturn's long year.
